title: Visible light-assisted thermal catalytic reverse water gas reaction over Cu-CeO2: The synergistic of hot electrons and oxygen vacancies induced by LSPR effect
abstract: The construction of a light-assisted thermal catalytic system has great potential in the reverse water gas shift reaction (RWGS). To explore the role of light in the thermo-catalytic system, a prepared Cu-CeO2 sample was performed for the RWGS reaction under visible light irradiation. It was found that Cu-CeO2 sample shows an excellent RWGS catalytic activity and CO selectivity, and the production of CO with light introduction has been significantly increased by 30 % at 250 °C. A combination of In-situ DRIFTS, Quasi-situ EPR, and XPS characterization results demonstrate that under visible light irradiation, the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) produced by Cu nanoparticles stimulates hot electrons transfer and attack to the bidentate formats and linear-CO intermediate species, resulting in that accelerating the decomposition and desorption of intermediate species into CO, but inhibiting further reduction of CO. Moreover, the spillover of H2 from Cu to CeO2 surface is also affected by light due to the observed regeneration of oxygen vacancies on the CeO2 surface, which together influence the yield of CO. This work shows that introducing visible light could improve RWGS reaction activity and retain the selectivity of CO, which maybe provide a new approach to control the product selectivity for a thermal catalytic reaction.
paragraphs: The continuous increase of CO2 emissions will cause serious natural disasters, which arouse widespread concern[1], [2]. In recent years, more efforts have been made to realize the conversion of CO2 into chemicals and fuels[3], [4]. Among them, the use of CO2 hydrogenation technology to catalyze the reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reaction (CO2 + H2 → CO + H2O) to produce CO is of great significance, which provides raw materials for the Fischer-Tropsch process to produce high value-added fuels[5], [6], [7]. A suitable catalyst can provide an ideal platform for CO2 to adsorb and dissociate under mild reaction conditions. Nevertheless, relying solely on thermal energy to catalyze RWGS still consumes a lot of energy and brings a certain degree of environmental problems[8].

Photo-thermal synergistic catalysis provides a new way to efficiently catalyze the RWGS reaction. An appropriate wavelength of light can excite the semiconductor to generate photo-generated carriers and cause the regular migration of electrons, which directly affects the adsorption and activation of CO2[9]. Lee et al[9] reported that the photo-electrons from the conduction band of catalyst could transfer to the LUMO orbital of CO2 to generate OC•O−, resulting in activation CO2. Qi et al[10] verify that the existence of oxygen vacancies can adjust the electronic structure which strengthens the light-harvesting and chemical adsorption of CO2 in photo-thermal RWGS reaction. It is also worth noting that the change of charge distribution may cause changes to the energy barrier and reaction path in the catalytic reaction. For instance, Li et al[11] synthesize the single-unit-cell layers CuIn5S8 and confirm that under visible light the charge-enriched Cu-In dual-site not only lowers the activation energy but also changes the step on reaction process. Wang et al[12] also confirmed that under UV light irradiation, the different photo-electrons transfer routes change the reaction route in CO2 methanation reaction. In our previous work[13], we also found that photo-excited electron transfer is beneficial to the adsorption and dissociation of CO2 and the regeneration of oxygen vacancies, thereby increasing the rate of the CO2 methanation reaction.

In addition to light-excited semiconductors that cause changes in the electron distribution on the catalyst surface, the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) of metals is also not negligible. Compare to direct light-excited semiconductors, the hot charge carriers generated by LSPR possess higher energies[14], [15]. Metals with the LSPR effect can excite high-energy hot electrons through the oscillation of electrons under light excitation. High-energy hot electrons can be injected into CO2, which promotes the conversion and desorption of CO2, thereby greatly increasing the reaction rate[16], [17]. Au, Ag, Cu, are considered to be the most promising materials due to their visible-light-induced LSPR effect and photocatalytic activity. Tahir et al[18] reported that under visible light irradiation, the plasmon-excited hot electrons which possess sufficient energy can transfer from Au to TiO2 to reduce CO2. Aniruddha et al [19] also through kinetics confirm that the LSPR changes the intrinsic reaction kinetics on the catalyst surface and the hot electrons can transfer to the adsorbed species which accelerates the desorption of products in the RWGS reaction. Moreover, Ge et al[20] clarify that the surface O vacancies and plasmonic adsorption play a critical role in the CO2 hydrogenation reaction. Cu as a kind of non-precious metal has been widely applied in the thermal catalytic reaction of CO2 hydrogenation and has excellent low-temperature activity and selectivity[21], [22]. Therefore, it is meaningful to combine the LSPR of Cu nanoparticles with their catalytic performance.

Here, Cu-CeO2 has been successfully applied to the photothermal synergistic catalysis RWGS reaction and the synergy mechanism has been studied. CeO2 as a typical reducible rare earth metal oxide has received much attention in CO2 hydrogenation due to the efficient transition between the Ce3+ and Ce4+ oxidation which formed oxygen vacancies structural defects that can effectively dissociative activation of CO2[23], [24]. Cu causes LSPR to excite hot electrons under visible light, which facilitates the decomposition of hydrogen and can decompose the surface formate species into CO. Moreover, hydrogen overflow promotes the regeneration of oxygen vacancies on the CeO2 surface and strengthens the re-adsorption of CO2. We used In-situ DRIFTS, Quasi-situ EPR, and H2-pulse-MS characterization to detect the reaction process, and the detailed reaction mechanism of Cu and cerium oxide was proposed.

As described in the previous literature[21], [25]. Ceria rod supports were prepared by a hydrothermal method. To obtain ceria rod support, 1.96 g of Ce(NO3)3·6H2O and 16.8 g of NaOH were dissolved in 40 mL deionized water and 30 mL deionized water, respectively. Subsequently, the NaOH solution was added dropwise into the Ce(NO3) solution and stirred for 1 h, then the resultant slurry was introduced into a stainless steel autoclave and kept at 373 K for 24 h. After the autoclave cooling down to room temperature, centrifuging and washing to get the precipitate. Finally, after the precursor was dried, ceria rod supports were obtained by calcined the precursor in the air at 400 °C for 4 h

For the preparation of Cu-CeO2 catalysts, a series of Cu-CeO2 catalysts with different loadings (2.5 wt%, 5.0 wt%, 7.5 wt%, 10.0 wt%) was synthesized using the wet impregnation method[24]. Specifically, the as-prepared CeO2 powder and different amounts of Cu(NO3)2·3H2O were dissolved into 20 mL of ethanol with ultrasound 0.5 h, then the obtained mixture was dried overnight under the water bath at 60 °C. Subsequently, the mixture was placed in a muffle furnace and calcined at 400 °C for 1.5 h to obtain CuO-CeO2 catalyst. Finally, the Cu-CeO2 catalyst was obtained by H2 reduction at 350 °C for 1 h.

The RWGS reaction performance over the Cu-CeO2 was evaluated by a fixed-bed flow reactor (seeing Fig. S1 in supporting information (SI)). Typically, about 240 mg catalyst (60–120 mesh) was placed in the quartz tube reactor (15 mm × 30 mm × 1 mm). Prior to the reaction, the catalysts were reduced under the H2 atmosphere at 350 °C for 1 h. The ratio of reaction gas was set at 1:4 (CO2: H2). Under dark reaction conditions, the catalytic of RWGS activity was evaluated at 210, 230, 250, and 270 °C, respectively. During the photo-thermal reaction process, visible light was introduced into the reaction system. The visible light was supplied by Xe lamp using UV-IR cut-off filter to remove UV and IR light which wavelengths below 420 nm and above 760 nm. The outlet gas concentration was analyzed by chromatography (Agilent 7890B, TDX-01) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector and flame ionization detector.

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of the catalysts was performed on a Bruker D8 Advance powder X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα irradiation (40 kV, 40 mA). XRD patterns were recorded from 20 to 85° with a step size of 0.1°. The optical properties of the as-prepared were determined by UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) using a UV-vis spectrophotometer (Agilent, Cary 5000) with BaSO4 as a reference. The charge separation rate was analyzed by photoluminescence (PL) spectra characterization using Hitachi F-7000 with the excitation wavelength of 350 nm. The morphology of the catalyst was characterized by TEM and HRTEM using a JEM-2100F field-emission transmission electron microscopy operating at 200 kV. Textual properties were characterized by recording N2 physisorption isotherms using a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 surface area analysis instrument. ICP-OES was performed on an Agilent 720 instrument to measure the actual content of Cu. The Autohem II 2920 (Micromeritics) was used to investigate the reducibility of catalyst by temperature-programmed reduction (TPR). The exposed copper metallic sites of Cu-CeO2 catalyst were also characterized by Autohem II 2920 (Micromeritics) instrument. The temperature-programmed surface reaction (TPSR), H2-pulse and H2-pulse-MS were also characterized by Autohem II 2920 (Micromeritics) instrument. Typically, The chemical composition and chemical state of the as-prepared catalyst were investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) using a Thermo ESCALAB 250XI with Al-Kɑ X-ray source. The binding-energy values of the XPS spectra was calibrated by using C 1 s (284.80 eV) as a standard. The electrochemical characterization was performed on PGSTAT204 electrochemical workstation with a standard three-electrode cell.

The Quasi-situ electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) was performed on the Bruke A300 instrument to explore the unpaired electrons and structural properties of the catalyst under dark and light conditions. The magnetic field strength during the characterization is 15 dB, the power of the instrument is 6.35 mW, and the frequency of the microwave bridge is 9.84 GHz. The visible light source used was consistent with the performance evaluation.

Due to the O2 can formed to O2– species and other free radical active species after O2 accepting electrons, thus, we used O2 as probe molecule[26]. Typically, 10 mg of the as-prepared catalysts (60–120 mesh) was pretreated reduction by 10% H2-Ar gas atmosphere at 350 °C for 1 h. When the temperature cooled down to 250 °C, the O2 or CO2 + O2 was introduced into the system and then the EPR test was started.

In-situ DRIFTS experiments were measured using an in-situ chamber (Harrick) equipped with ZnSe windows. The spectra were recorded from 1000 to 3500 cm−1 using Bruker V880 FTIR instrument equipped with an MCT detector (cooled by liquid N2 at 77 K). Prior to characterization, the as-prepared catalyst was pre-reduced by hydrogen (10 vol% H2–Ar, 40 mL min−1) at 350 °C for 1 h, and then cooled down to 30 °C. The gas flow was changed to pure CO2 at 30 °C and adsorbed for 1 h. When the CO2 adsorption is saturated, change the gas flow to H2 and recording the spectrum from 30 °C to 350 °C with a ramping rate of 10 °C min−1. For the In-situ DRIFTS experiments under light conditions, visible light was introduced into the experiment system after the H2 pre-treat. The visible light source used was consistent with the performance evaluation.

A series of Cu-CeO2 catalysts with different loadings (2.5 wt%, 5.0 wt%, 7.5 wt%, 10.0 wt%) were prepared by the wet impregnation method. The detailed preparation method is described in section 2. Prior to catalytic characterization, the as-prepared catalyst was pre-treated reduced under H2 atmosphere at 350 °C for 1 h. XRD patterns of the as-prepared catalysts are shown in Fig. S2 in SI. The 2θ diffraction peaks at 28.5°, 33.1°, 47.5°, 56.3°, 59.1° and 69.4° correspond to the (111), (200), (220), (311), (222) and (400) planes of the CeO2(PDF#34-0394), respectively. The XRD analysis indicates that CeO2 and Cu-CeO2 could be classified into fluorite cubic structure CeO2. When increasing the loadings of Cu, there appears a characteristic Cu peak of the (111) plane, indicating that Cu is successfully loaded on the CeO2.

The morphology of Cu-CeO2 was observed by TEM (Fig. 1). As shown in Fig. 1a, it can be seen that Cu nanoparticles of about 5 nm are loaded on CeO2 nanorods. From the HRTEM image (Fig. 1b), the lattice fringes of 0.31 and 0.30 nm are attributed to the (111) and (110) planes of CeO2 and Cu2O, respectively. Unfortunately, we did not observe the lattice fringes of Cu due to the inevitable occurrence of Cu oxidation during the test. The EDX and Mapping images (Fig. 1c and d) further demonstrate that the existence of Ce, O, Cu species on the Cu-CeO2 catalyst.

The metal content and textual information of the as-prepared catalysts are listed in Table 1. The ICP-OES analysis indicates that actual metal loading in all catalysts is close to the target value. The textual information demonstrates that the as-prepared catalysts are mesoporous materials and cover a wide range of BET areas from 77–104 m2·gcat−1. Nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms as shown in Fig. S3 in SI. The result reveals that the catalysts are typical type IV with H3 hysteresis loop.

UV-vis spectra of CeO2 and Cu-CeO2 indicate that the absorption band edge of as-prepared catalysts is close to 400 nm (Fig. 2). From the spectra, Cu-CeO2 has an obvious peak around 640 nm, which is ascribed to the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) peak of Cu. This result demonstrates that visible light (420–780 nm) can excite the plasmon effect of Cu. Moreover, the samples with different Cu loading amount exhibit different light absorption ability which caused by the LSPR effect of Cu nanoparticle[27] (Fig. S4 in SI).

The performance of photo-thermal catalysis RWGS reaction over the Cu-CeO2 was evaluated by a fixed-bed flow reactor under visible light irradiation (420–780 nm). Prior to the performance test, the catalysts were reduced under H2 atmosphere at 350 °C for 1 h. Subsequently, the catalytic activity of the RWGS reaction with different loading was evaluated in the temperature range of 210–270 °C under the mixed reaction gas (CO2: H2 = 1: 4) and space velocity of 14250 mL g−1h−1 (GHSV). The TOF of product evolution with temperature under dark and visible light conditions are depicted in Fig. 3.

In this study, the catalysts were found to be 100% selective for CO product with different temperatures. As shown in Fig. 3a, when introducing visible light, 5.0 wt%Cu-CeO2 shows the most obvious visible light promoted performance at 250 °C. Therefore, in order to further explore the influence of Cu loadings on the visible promotes catalytic activity, the different Cu loadings performance evaluation was employed at 250 °C. The result as shown in Fig. 3b, When the reaction temperature at 250 °C, the visible light promotes RWGS reaction performance shows a volcanic type change trend with increment of Cu loadings. 5.0 wt% Cu-CeO2 exhibits the best light-promoted activity, which the CO product is increased by 30% under visible light irradiation. This may be due to the low content of Cu cannot provide enough active sites and hot electrons which induced by the LSPR effect of Cu nanoparticles to promote the RWGS reaction, while the excessive Cu causes the Cu nanoparticle aggregation on the catalyst surface thus decrease the RWGS reaction performance. Note that the catalytic activity of samples seems not to be consistent with the light absorption ability (Fig. S4). This may be due to the higher loading of Cu causing the Cu nanoparticle aggregation and inhibiting the generation of hot electrons [27], [28], [29]. Therefore, we selected 5.0 wt% Cu-CeO2 catalyst as the research object and conducted light intensity experiments to further confirm the visible light has a positive influence to the performance of the RWGS reaction. As shown in Fig. 3c, the activity of RWGS reaction was improved with the light intensity enhanced. And the surface temperature of 5.0 wt%Cu-CeO2 at 250 °C also was detected by a thermal imager. As shown in Fig. S5, the surface temperature of catalyst does not increase significantly under visible light irradiation. These results suggest that the visible light promotes performance maybe cause by hot electrons, not the thermal effect. Moreover, 5.0 wt%Cu-CeO2 catalyst shows excellent stability after the 1800 min test under visible light conditions, completely. (Fig. 3d) Moreover, we have calculated the activation energies of RWGS reaction according to the Arrhenius formula under thermal and photo-thermal conditions (Fig. S6 in SI). The apparent activation energy value of the photo-thermal process was 36.65 KJ/mol which is obviously below the thermal process (53.03 KJ/mol). This result indicated that the visible light induced LSPR was mainly responsible for the visible light promoting RWGS reaction over Cu-CeO2.

Although apart from CO, we did not detect other reduction products through the TCD and FID detector, but we detected CH3OH product by H2-pulse-MS test. As shown in Fig. 4 and Fig. S7 in SI, the m/z = 15 and m/z = 32 ascribed the MS signal of CH3OH. The MS signal of CH3OH is obviously decreased under visible light irradiation, indicating that the visible-light-induced LSPR effect suppresses CO to be further reduced thus promoting the generation of CO and retaining the selectivity of CO.

H2 temperature-programmed reduction (H2-TPR) was employed to investigate the redox properties of the as-prepared catalysts. As shown in Fig. 5a, the reduction temperature of CuO is about 294 °C. When Cu is loaded on the surface of CeO2, the reduction temperature is significantly reduced to within 150 °C. The peak located at 82 °C and 127 °C is ascribed to the well dispersion CuO on the CeO2 surface and the surface CuOX species interacting with CeO2, respectively[22]. And the high-temperature reduction peak (144 °C) can be attributed to the reduction of bulk CuO[30]. This implies that there exists metal-support interaction (SMSI) between Cu and CeO2[22]. The result also demonstrates that the CuO has completely reduced to Cu under 350 °C before performance evaluation. And, we also find the CeO2 cannot be reduced under 350 °C. It further confirms that all three reduction peaks are ascribed to Cu.

The Cu sites on the surface play a crucial role in the RWGS reaction. We used a combined H2-N2O-TPR method to measure the exposed copper metallic sites of the Cu-CeO2 catalyst (Fig. 5b). First, we employ H2-TPR measurement and the peak area of the test result is marked as S1. Then, we use N2O to oxidation the Cu on the CeO2 surface. Finally, we employ H2-TPR measurement again, and the peak area of the test result is marked as S2. According to the measurement result and the dispersion formula (D = 2S2/S1), we calculate the dispersion of Cu is approximately 40% (Fig. 5b). This result implies that there have many exposed copper metallic sites on Cu-CeO2 catalyst thus provides many reaction active sites and accelerates the RWGS reaction.

Much previous literature reported that oxygen vacancies play an important role in CO2 capture[31], [32]. Quasi-situ electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) was employed to investigate the changes of oxygen vacancy during the reaction. As shown in Fig. 6a [33], the EPR peak located at g||=2.031, g⊥=2.007 is ascribed to O2− signal which is connected with Ce4+[33], [34]. This may be because oxygen serves as probe molecules to fill the oxygen vacancies and the Ce3+ donates electrons simultaneously (Ce3+ − VO¨ + O2 → Ce4+ − O2−)[35]. The EPR peak located at g1 = 2.041 is ascribed to the signal of oxygen vacancies[34]. When we introduce visible light into the characterization process, we found that three EPR signal peaks intensity is all enhanced obviously, and appeared a new signal peak located at g2 = 1.966 which belongs to Ce3+ species[34], [36]. We speculate that the reason for the enhanced peak intensity under visible light may be that the LSPR effect of Cu nanoparticles promotes H2 spillover and thus takes oxygen away from the CeO2 surface to produce oxygen vacancies. Collins and Mukherjee[37], [38] reported that the LSPR of Au nanoparticles can accelerate the spillover of H2, and the spillover of H2 is easier to take away the O on the surface. The H2-pulse characterization also confirms that the LSPR effect of Cu can accelerate the spillover of H2 under visible light irradiation (Fig. S8 in SI). Subsequently, in order to explore the relationship between oxygen vacancies and CO2 during the reaction process. We inject CO2 into the EPR tube after pretreating the catalyst with hydrogen and then inject O2 probe molecules to employ Quasi-situ electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) characterization. As displayed in Fig. 6b, there is still no EPR signal after H2 pretreatment. When CO2 and O2 were injected, three EPR signals also appeared which the signal position was consistent with the above before. However, the signal intensity is clearly decreased. This may be due to the adsorption of CO2 on the oxygen vacancies thus resulting in the decrease of oxygen vacancies. Similarly, after introduced visible light, the EPR signal intensity increase significantly, and there was also appeared a new signal peak located at g2 = 1.966 which is ascribed to Ce3+ species. This result further proves that visible light is beneficial to the regeneration of oxygen vacancies, which is consistent with the previous conclusions.

In the light excitation process, the generation and transfer of photo-electrons could change the local electron density which plays an important role in CO2 activation. To further investigate the changes in the surface elemental composition and chemical state of the catalyst during the reaction, we perform XPS and Cu LMM Auger characterization (Fig. 7a and b). Under the dark condition, Cu 2p core-level spectra show obvious signals at a binding energy of 932.41 eV and 952.27 eV corresponding to Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2, respectively[39], [40]. The shake-up peaks that appeared at 937–948 eV indicated the presence of Cu2+. According to the previous literature reported, the XPS peak located at 932.41 eV and 952.27 eV is generally attributed to the reduced copper species (Cu0 or Cu+)[41]. As we all know, due to the similar peak and position of Cu0 and Cu+, it is difficult to distinguish the Cu0 and Cu+ species according to XPS fine spectrum. Therefore, in order to determine the chemical state of Cu, we employed Cu LMM Auger electron spectroscopy to identify them. As shown in Fig. 7b, there was only one peak at 918.7 eV corresponded to Cu0 species. Thus, we infer that during the dark reaction, the Cu0 is mainly species in the Cu-CeO2 surface and Cu0 nanoparticles are the active site for the RWGS reaction[23]. After the visible light was introduced, we found that the XPS peak of Cu 2p shifted to higher binding energy, indicating that during the photo-thermal reaction process, Cu nanoparticles will give out electrons. This may be due to the visible light excited the LSPR effect of Cu nanoparticles and generate hot electrons, and at the same time, the hot electrons happened migration during the photo-thermal reaction process. Similarly, the Cu LMM Auger electron spectroscopy (Fig. 7b) after the photo-thermal reaction also verify the above conclusions.

The Ce 3d spectra are rather complicated. The spectrum could be fitted into ten peaks, because the spin-orbit split of the 3d5/2 and 3d3/2 core levels, [42], [43]. As shown in Fig. 8a, the red and blue colors represent Ce4+ and Ce3+ ions, respectively. The concentration of Ce3+ was positively correlated with oxygen vacancies. Thus, we calculate the concentration of Ce3+ under different reaction conditions by formula 1–1. The result display in Table 2, the concentration of Ce3+ under H2 pretreatment is the most. After the dark reaction, the content of Ce3+ is obviously decreased, and the concentration of Ce3+ was increasing significantly after the visible light was introduced. As shown in Fig. 8b and Table 2, the concentration of adsorbed oxygen under dark conditions is also lower than that under light conditions, which was consistent with the EPR result. This result suggests that under dark reaction conditions, the introduction of CO2 could occupy oxygen vacancies and forming intermediates, thus decreasing the number of oxygen vacancies. However, when we introduce the visible light, the visible-light-induced Cu generated the LSPR effect, and the LSPR of Cu accelerate the spillover of H2, thus generate more oxygen vacancies.ConcentrationofCe3+=∑peakareaofCe3+∑peakareaof(Ce3++Ce4+)

The interfacial electron transfer in Cu-CeO2 was further confirmed by electrochemical and photoluminescence (PL) characterization (Fig. 9). As shown in Fig. 9a, under visible light irradiation, CeO2 support does not exhibit a photocurrent signal, but Cu-CeO2 exhibits an obvious photocurrent signal. This indicates that CeO2 support is not responsive to visible light, however, visible light can excite the LSPR effect of Cu and generate hot electrons. EIS Nyquist plots of the as-prepared demonstrate that Cu-CeO2 exhibits much better electron mobility (Fig. 9b). The PL spectra further confirm that after introducing visible light, the hot electrons generated by the LSPR effect of Cu can be effectively separated and transferred (Fig. 9c).

In order to further explore the adsorption pathway and reaction mechanism of CO2 and H2 in the reaction process, in-situ DRIFTS IR was applied with or without visible light. As shown in Fig. 10, under dark reaction conditions, there appear four obvious absorption peaks at 1370, 2845–2965, 2118, and 2350 cm−1, respectively. The assignment of in-situ DRIFTS IR absorbance peaks is summarized in Table 3. The absorption peaks at 1370 cm−1 and 2845–2965 cm−1 ascribe to the OCO stretching vibration of bidentate formate (HCOO*) and CH stretching vibration[23], [44], respectively. The others at 2350 cm−1 and ∼2118 cm−1 correspond to gaseous CO2 and linear adsorption CO peak (L-CO) which adsorbed on Cu[45]. From Fig. 10a, we can found that the signal of bidentate formate (HCOO–) and linear adsorption CO was increased with reaction temperature increase. This demonstrates that there is more bidentate formate (HCOO*) formed on the catalyst surface and the formed bidentate formate (HCOO*) further decomposes to CO which adsorb on Cu.

Under the light condition, when introduction visible light, the intensity of bidentate formate (HCOO*) species is significantly stronger than dark reaction. It can be inferred that the introduction of visible light facilitates the adsorption of CO2 and benefits the conversion of the intermediate carbon species to bidentate formate (HCOO*). In the above quasi-situ EPR、XPS study, we confirm that the introduction of visible light could increase the number of oxygen vacancies by the LSPR effect of Cu. Therefore, we speculate that after the introduction of visible light, the LSPR effect of Cu enhances hydrogen spillover, thus generating more oxygen vacancies, which is beneficial to the adsorption of CO2 on the oxygen vacancies and formed bidentate formate intermediate carbon species. When the reaction temperature rises, the intensity of bidentate formate gradually weakens. This may be due to the hot electrons generated by the LSPR effect of metallic Cu attack the bidentate formate, hence it is beneficial to the cleavage of the bidentate formate into CO. However, it is interesting that the liner CO species (L-CO) adsorption peak is significantly weakened or even disappeared after visible light irradiation. This suggests that the hot electrons generated by the LSPR effect of Cu facilitate the desorption of linear CO (L-CO). We also employed temperature-programmed surface reaction (TPSR-MS) to further investigate the interaction of CO2 and H2. As shown in Fig. S9 in SI, we found that the MS signal intensity of CO and H2O are all enhanced under visible light. This result further demonstrated that under visible light conditions, the performance of reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reaction was promoted.

According to the literature[46], [47], there are two reaction mechanisms of RWGS reaction that have been widely accepted, namely, redox mechanism and decomposition intermediate species mechanism. Based on the above analysis, we propose a possible mechanism, as shown in Fig. 11. Under the dark condition, the reaction process proceeds as follows five steps: (Ⅰ) First, H2 dissociatively on Cu site. (Ⅱ) CO2 reacts with the oxygen vacancies on cerium oxide. (III) H2 dissociate and spill over the H atoms to the intermediate, leading to formed bidentate formats (HCOO*) intermediate species. (Ⅳ) bidentate formats (HCOO*) dissociation to CO、adsorbed OH and linear CO (L-CO) which adsorption on Cu. (Ⅴ) linear CO (L-CO) desorption to CO and the formed OH reacts with H atom to form H2O. The above react step demonstrates that the activation of CO2 over Cu-CeO2 does not occur through the redox mechanism which directs dissociation of CO2 to CO and O on the Cu particles, but occurs decomposition intermediate species mechanism. As depicted in Fig. 11, we display one possible mechanism by which LSPR can accelerate the reaction step. When introducing visible light, the hot electrons generated by the LSPR of Cu attack the bidentate formats (HCOO*) intermediate species and linear CO (L-CO) which accelerate the HCOO* decomposition and the L-CO desorption. According to EPR、XPS and In-situ DRIFTS analysis, we speculate that under visible light irradiation, the LSPR of Cu enhances the number of oxygen vacancies which is beneficial to generate HCOO*.

Therefore, we conclude two possible roles of the LSPR effect to the RWGS reaction performance: on the one hand, the visible light excited the LSPR effect of Cu and strength the hydrogen spillover phenomenon, thus generate more oxygen vacancies on the surface of the catalyst which beneficial CO2 convert to bidentate formats (HCOO*) intermediate species. And on the other hand, the hot electrons generated by the LSPR effect attack the bidentate formats (HCOO*) intermediate species and linear CO (L-CO), which is beneficial to decompose the bidentate formats (HCOO*) to CO and desorption of linear CO (L-CO) species. Thus, the visible light promoted the performance of reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reaction was achieved.
The detailed RWGS reaction mechanism via bidentate formats (HCOO*) as intermediate species was displayed in Fig. 11, and the possible reaction steps are inferred as follows:
Dark reaction mechanism:
H2 dissociatively on Cu site
CO2 reacts with the oxygen vacancies on cerium oxide and the H atoms spill over to the intermediate, formed bidentate formats (HCOO*) intermediate species, simultaneously.
Bidentate formats (HCOO*) dissociation to CO、adsorbed OH and linear CO (L-CO) which adsorption on Cu.
Linear CO (L-CO) desorption to CO and the formed OH reacts with H atom to form H2O.
Visible light promotes reaction mechanism:
Visible light induce the plasmon effect of Cu to generate hot electrons and hot holes
The hot holes react with hydrogen to accelerate hydrogen dissociation and spillover
The hot electrons transfer and attack to the intermediate species to generate CO
The oxygen vacancies regenerate under visible light irradiation

Overall, Cu-CeO2 has been successfully prepared and exhibits excellent visible light promoted performance in the RWGS reaction at 250 °C. Moreover, Quasi-situ EPR, XPS, in-situ DRIFTS IR and TPSR-MS characterization confirm that the oxygen vacancies participate in CO2 adsorption and activation through bidentate formats (HCOO*) as intermediates. The introduction of visible light inducing the LSPR effect of Cu, accelerates the generation of oxygen vacancies and decomposition of bidentate formats (HCOO*), thus promoted the performance of RWGS reaction. The findings unravel the crucial roles of the LSPR effect in the photothermal RWGS reaction.
